messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 76
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Radiologist
  trauma_type: Civilian in war zone
  pcl5: 63

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid All Feelings: avoid anything that could cause negative or positive feelings, Avoid Future Plans: Making any plans for the future, Screen Escape: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking
  Threat: Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
  Memory: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Miriam Calloway is a 76-year-old married radiologist who presented for an initial psychological evaluation following a traumatic experience as a civilian caught in an active war zone approximately fourteen months ago. She had traveled abroad to assist with a humanitarian medical mission, lending her diagnostic expertise to an understaffed regional hospital. Within days of her arrival, the area came under sustained aerial bombardment. Miriam spent nearly three weeks sheltering in a partially collapsed building alongside local medical staff and civilians, moving through corridors lit only by emergency lanterns, reading scans on a battery-powered laptop while the walls shuddered around her. She witnessed injuries she could not treat, and she was present when decisions were made — decisions she was asked to inform with her imaging reads — that she has never been able to fully articulate since. What happened in those final days before evacuation remains, for Miriam, something closer to a physical sensation than a story she can tell. When she attempts to reconstruct those events deliberately, she finds herself reaching for something that recedes, as though the memory exists only as texture and pressure rather than sequence or language. She cannot put it into words, she told her intake clinician, and the shame that rises when she tries — a hot, flooding sense that she failed in some fundamental way — makes her stop trying almost immediately.

In the months following her return to the United States, Miriam continued working part-time at a hospital radiology department, reading films remotely from a home workstation. What had once been solitary, focused work became something she dreaded. The reading room at the hospital, when she occasionally went in, required her to pass through a busy corridor, and she found herself pausing at the entrance to scan the hallway before stepping through — noting exits, watching the posture of strangers, calculating. When a hospital porter she did not recognize rounded a corner toward her one afternoon, she pressed herself against the wall, heart hammering, before she consciously registered that she was in suburban Ohio. She stopped going in after that. She told her husband it was more efficient to work from home, and he accepted this without question, though she noticed him watching her sometimes.

At home, Miriam has constructed her days around the avoidance of anything that might move her emotionally — in either direction. She does not watch films with her husband anymore, does not open letters from former colleagues, does not make plans for the holidays or for retirement, which she had previously been approaching with quiet anticipation. The idea of planning forward, of imagining herself in a future, feels to her somehow presumptuous and dangerous, as though the future is a place she has forfeited the right to inhabit with confidence. She has not returned to the book club she attended for eleven years. When her daughter called to discuss a family gathering, Miriam said she would see how she felt, and then did not call back.

In place of these things, she spends hours on her phone — scrolling, playing simple word games, moving through one application to the next. She described this to her clinician with visible embarrassment, noting that she was a physician and understood, abstractly, what she was doing. But the screen, she said, keeps her just below the surface of things. It asks nothing of her and takes her nowhere she does not choose to go. Unfamiliar places have come to feel categorically unsafe; she has not been to her usual grocery store since it was renovated, because the new layout means she cannot immediately read the exits.

What finally brought Miriam to seek help was a conversation with her husband of forty-eight years, who told her gently that he felt he had lost her. She did not argue with him. She came to her first appointment saying very little about what she hoped for, except that she wanted to be able to sit in a room with the people she loved and not be somewhere else entirely. What she feared most, she said quietly, was that what she carried was not something that could be approached — that if she ever found the words for it, the shame would confirm what she already suspected about herself.
